title: Spontaneous Remission in Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria: An Extremely Rare Case
content: To the Editor,Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal disease with the main clinical manifestations of hemolytic anemia, bone marrow failure, and thrombophilia [1]. While it was previously reported that spontaneous remission develops in 15%-30% of patients with PNH, this rate is as low as 3% in recent studies [2,3,4,5]. This inconsistency between results is probably due to the differences in the definitions of “spontaneous remission” used in these studies and the analysis methods applied. Herein, we present a rare case of aplastic anemia/PNH overlap syndrome where the patient achieved remission under immunosuppressive and anticomplement therapy.In 2012, a 24-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital due to severe fatigue. Pancytopenia was detected in the complete blood count. Biochemical analysis was normal, except for a slight increase in lactate dehydrogenase and a low haptoglobin level. Bone marrow biopsy revealed decreased bone marrow cellularity (40%) and relative erythroid hyperplasia. A flow cytometric evaluation revealed a PNH granulocyte clone size of 56.3%. The patient was started on eculizumab treatment, which continued for 6 years. PNH clone percentages and clinical parameters over the years are shown in Table 1. The PNH clone size gradually decreased from 56.3% to 12.96% under eculizumab treatment. Repeated bone marrow biopsy revealed a decrease in cellularity to 35% and, due to the tendency of a decreasing platelet count, cyclosporine was added to the treatment at 200 mg/day. After 1 year of combined treatment, the pancytopenia was resolved, PNH clone size had decreased to 4.86%, and follow-up bone marrow biopsy showed an increase in cellularity (65%). With these results, eculizumab and cyclosporine treatment was discontinued in 2019. The PNH clone size of the patient, who is still asymptomatic 27 months after the cessation of treatment, continues to shrink. During the entire clinical course, the patient did not need transfusions and no complications related to PNH developed.The disappearance of the PNH clone may be due to various causes, such as complete recovery, deepening of bone marrow aplasia, or transformation to leukemia. However, the underlying mechanisms and the reasons for complete recovery are unknown. One of the hypotheses put forward is that clones of cells affected by PNH have a limited lifespan like normal somatic cells [3]. There are also cases in the literature that draw attention to the relationship between pathological PNH clones and bone marrow environmental conditions [6,7]. Recent studies have shown that PNH is a multiclonal disease and hosts additional somatic mutations that result in a complex hierarchical clonal architecture similar to that observed in myeloid neoplasms. Thus, it has been suggested that remission of PNH may occur through the emergence of a new dominant clone carrying multiple somatic mutations rather than restoration of normal hematopoiesis [5,8,9]. As a result, the highly variable clinical spectrum of PNH is also reflected in cases of remission. Understanding the underlying pathophysiology of this extremely rare condition will form the basis for the development of curative treatments for the disease.

diagnosis.disease_name: Aplastic anemia/PNH overlap syndrome (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria)
diagnosis.severity_description: pancytopenia with decreased bone marrow cellularity; severe fatigue; mild hemolysis markers (slightly increased LDH, low haptoglobin)
diagnosis.lab_values: Bone marrow cellularity 40% initially; slight LDH increase; low haptoglobin; PNH granulocyte clone 56.3% initially; later 12.96% then 4.86%; marrow cellularity decreased to 35% then increased to 65%

treatment.treatments_raw: Eculizumab (anti-complement therapy) for 6 years; cyclosporine 200 mg/day added due to decreasing platelet count; both discontinued in 2019
treatment.treatment_stopped_reason: With resolution of pancytopenia, shrinking PNH clone, and improved marrow cellularity, eculizumab and cyclosporine were discontinued in 2019

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: Gradual decrease in clone over 6 years on eculizumab; after 1 year of combined eculizumab + cyclosporine pancytopenia resolved and clone decreased to 4.86%
remission_outcome.verification_detail: Serial flow cytometry showed PNH granulocyte clone shrinking (56.3% → 12.96% → 4.86%) and continuing to shrink after stopping therapy; CBC pancytopenia resolved; bone marrow biopsies showed cellularity changes (40% → 35% → 65%)
remission_outcome.tumor_response: PNH clone size progressively decreased and continued shrinking after stopping treatment; pancytopenia resolved
remission_outcome.biomarker_trajectory: PNH granulocyte clone 56.3% (2012) → 12.96% (under eculizumab) → 4.86% (after 1 year combined therapy); pancytopenia resolved
remission_outcome.tissue_regeneration_detail: Bone marrow cellularity increased to 65% on follow-up biopsy after combined treatment

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: Article states spontaneous remission is extremely rare in recent studies (~3%).
validation.extraction_notes: Remission described occurred after years of eculizumab and cyclosporine; although titled 'spontaneous remission', case appears compatible with gradual remission under/after therapy rather than no-treatment regression.

analysis.case_summary: A 24-year-old woman diagnosed in 2012 with aplastic anemia/PNH overlap (pancytopenia, marrow hypocellularity, PNH granulocyte clone 56.3%) was treated with eculizumab for 6 years, then eculizumab plus cyclosporine. After 1 year of combination therapy pancytopenia resolved and marrow cellularity increased, and after stopping both drugs in 2019 she remained asymptomatic with continued shrinkage of the PNH clone at 27-month follow-up.
key_healing_factors: Anti-complement therapy with eculizumab over 6 years associated with gradual reduction in PNH clone size
Addition of cyclosporine (immunosuppression) associated with resolution of pancytopenia and improved marrow cellularity
Sustained improvement after discontinuation of therapy with continued clone shrinkage
unique_features: Longitudinal, quantified PNH clone reduction with serial marrow biopsies
Continued clone shrinkage and asymptomatic status 27 months after stopping eculizumab and cyclosporine
No transfusions required and no PNH complications during the course
analysis.analysis_notes: No psycho-spiritual factors, lifestyle changes, or anomalous experiences were described; the narrative is clinical and mechanistic. The remission is not 'pure spontaneous' because immunosuppressive and anticomplement therapies were administered and temporally associated with hematologic recovery.
